title: Redefining the utilisation of YouTube by life sciences teachers in the Fifth Industrial Revolution
text_snippet: Redefining the utilisation of YouTube by life sciences teachers in the Fifth Industrial Revolution YouTube has served as an online space wherein teachers interact with their learners through online videos. Over the past few years, standardised and unstandardised utilisation have dominated YouTube, while semi-standardized utilization has been neglected. Recently, life sciences teachers have gravitated towards the semi-standardised utilisation of YouTube, which allows for personal reflections and critiques. Despite different forms of utilisation, life sciences teachers have still been unable to optimise their teaching to achieve one hundred percent (100%) outcomes. In other words, either none of their learners achieve 100%, or not all of them do, even after the life sciences teachers have utilised YouTube videos. This suggests a problematic issue that needs to be addressed. As such, this study explores how life sciences teachers utilise YouTube nowadays. The main objectives of this study are to explore how Life Sciences teachers utilize YouTube and to understand why they utilize it in particular ways. title: Policy–practice gap in implementing competency-based curriculum in Southern African secondary schools
text_snippet: Policy–practice gap in implementing competency-based curriculum in Southern African secondary schools Competency-based curriculum (CBC) reforms have increasingly been adopted across Southern African education systems as governments attempt to improve learning outcomes, develop practical skills, and align schooling with contemporary socio-economic demands. Despite these policy ambitions, evidence from several education systems suggests that CBC reforms remain unevenly implemented, particularly in resource-constrained secondary schools, where institutional capacity and instructional resources are limited. This study examines the policy–practice gap in the implementation of competency-based curriculum in selected Southern African secondary schools by synthesising recent scholarly and policy literature. It employed a systematic literature review guided by PRISMA procedures to identify and analyse relevant studies published between 2020 and 2025. Search was conducted across major academic databases and policy repositories, yielding 25 studies that met the established inclusion criteria. The reviewed studies focused primarily on teachers, school administrators, and policy implementation in African secondary education systems. journal_name: International Journal of Studies in Inclusive Education
title: Exploring high school principals’ perceptions of the influence of school fees on inclusive education in Eswatini
text_snippet: Exploring high school principals’ perceptions of the influence of school fees on inclusive education in Eswatini Despite Eswatini’s policy commitment to inclusive education, high school principals are forced to rely on mandatory school fees to run their institutions, effectively creating an economic barrier that excludes marginalised and poor learners from accessing secondary education. This paper explores the experiences of two high school principals regarding school fee payments in the Manzini region, Eswatini. It further explores how mandatory school fees affect high school principals' ability to implement inclusive education practices for orphaned and vulnerable children and learners from low-income backgrounds in Eswatini. This study employed a qualitative phenomenological design, utilising semi-structured interviews for data collection and thematic analysis for data interpretation. Findings from this qualitative study indicate a critical policy–practice gap, in which the pressure to maintain institutional viability forces principals to adopt exclusionary financial measures. Consequently, while inclusive education is supported in theory, it is compromised in practice as financial solvency is prioritised over the universal right to access.

title: School governing body engagement as a catalyst for strengthening learner discipline in contexts of multiple deprivations
text_snippet: School governing body engagement as a catalyst for strengthening learner discipline in contexts of multiple deprivations Learner discipline remains a persistent challenge in South African schools, particularly in communities affected by multiple deprivations such as poverty, unemployment, family instability, substance abuse, and limited access to social support services. This study examined how School Governing Bodies (SGBs) strengthen learner discipline in secondary schools situated within such contexts. Guided by Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Social Capital Theory, the study explored how cultural norms, stakeholder relationships, and community engagement shape disciplinary practices and outcomes. A qualitative case study design was employed in two secondary schools in the King Cetshwayo District of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews with ten purposively selected participants, comprising school principals, School Management Team members, SGB chairpersons, parent representatives serving on SGBs, and members of the Representative Council of Learners. title: Graffiti as public pedagogy: Cross-institutional collaboration for student expression, healing, and transformation
text_snippet: Graffiti as public pedagogy: Cross-institutional collaboration for student expression, healing, and transformation Higher education in South Africa has been widely critiqued for privileging Eurocentric epistemologies that marginalise local knowledge systems and distance learning from the socio-political realities students inhabit. Such dynamics constrain students’ capacity to critically engage the historical and structural forces shaping identity, belonging, and wellbeing. Responding to these concerns, this study examines how a collaborative, arts-based pedagogical strategy centred on graffiti can advance more inclusive and socially responsive teaching practices for diverse student populations. Grounded in critical pedagogy and decolonial theory and informed by the group psychoanalytic concept of the social unconscious, the study conceptualises a graffiti installation as a participatory archive through which students explore the intersections of identity, power, place, and collective memory. A qualitative, participatory design was employed with 12 postgraduate students (7 psychology and 5 design students) across 2 private South African institutions. title: Pedagogical strategies for managing learner discipline in a virtual learning environment: A systematic literature review
text_snippet: Pedagogical strategies for managing learner discipline in a virtual learning environment: A systematic literature review The transition to digital education has intensified challenges in managing learner discipline within online settings, moving beyond traditional classroom management to a complex digital environment, where challenges such as disengagement, distraction, and lack of direct supervision prevail. This systematic literature review examines current research to identify evidence-based strategies that promote discipline, self-regulation, and sustained engagement in virtual learning environments. A systematic review of recent empirical studies was conducted, focusing on technology-enhanced learning, digital pedagogy, and online behaviour management. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search of the Scopus and Web of Science databases, including Google Scholar, for publications between 2020 and 2025 yielded 615 records, of which 24 high-quality studies met the inclusion criteria for in-depth thematic synthesis. Sources included peer-reviewed articles on gamification, artificial intelligence in education, collaborative online tasks, and learning analytics. title: Mentorship in open distance e-learning: Enhancing mentees’ academic development, career trajectories, and progress toward SDG 4
text_snippet: Mentorship in open distance e-learning: Enhancing mentees’ academic development, career trajectories, and progress toward SDG 4 New academics in higher education worldwide report high levels of stress from various sources. Adaptation and support through mentoring are needed if new academics engaged in teaching, research, and academic citizenship are to endure, learn, and contribute to student learning and advance in their academic careers. The need for support and development in academia through mentoring cannot be overstated, as it directly impacts advancing SDG#4. This has led to unravelling mentoring in academia as a vehicle for advancing SDG#4 in an Open Distance e-learning (ODeL) context. The effective mentorship programme in ODeL ensures that mentees are equipped with the academic skills to flourish in academia. The study explores mentees' mentorship experiences in an ODeL context to enhance their academic development, career trajectories, and SDG #4. This study employed a qualitative case study research design. Significantly, the study used the population. Fifteen new junior academics were purposively selected as mentees in an ODeL institution. title: Integrating indigenous rangeland knowledge with geographic information systems in fostering inclusive education through culturally responsive pedagogy
text_snippet: Integrating indigenous rangeland knowledge with geographic information systems in fostering inclusive education through culturally responsive pedagogy Across Sub-Saharan Africa, learner exclusion persists through curricula that silence indigenous ecological intelligence. This study argues that integrating indigenous rangeland knowledge with Geographic Information Systems (GIS) advances inclusive education and mediates learner behavior through culturally sustaining digital pedagogy. The research problem addresses how technology-mediated behaviour management strategies remain exclusive, privileging Western spatial frameworks and alienating learners from pastoralist communities. A systematic literature review methodology following PRISMA protocols was conducted for the study. Grounded in the culturally sustaining pedagogy and restorative practice theory, the study frames spatial justice as inseparable from behavioural inclusion. Findings reveal that when learners map indigenous grasing routes alongside satellite-derived vegetation indices, identity safety increases, disciplinary referrals decrease by 41%, and learners with learning disabilities demonstrate accelerated spatial cognition. title: Integrated AAC practices in school and home: Insights from Sekhukhune special schools, Limpopo province
text_snippet: Integrated AAC practices in school and home: Insights from Sekhukhune special schools, Limpopo province This study addresses the gap in effective collaboration and contextual adaptation in the use of Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) tools in resource-constrained rural schools, thereby limiting their consistent implementation for learners with complex communication needs. Drawing on a community engagement project led by the University of South Africa (Unisa), this qualitative study explores collaborative strategies among educators, therapists, and parents in five special schools in the Sekhukhune District, Limpopo Province. Using purposive sampling, data were collected from 17 participants through semi-structured interviews and reflective group discussions. Thematic analysis identified seven key themes, including shared communication goals, culturally responsive practices, and the integration of AAC across school and home. The findings reveal that teacher-parent-therapist collaboration is vital for consistent AAC use, enhancing learner independence and participation. title: Reframing disciplinary practices in inclusive education: Leadership role of departmental heads in South African schools
text_snippet: Reframing disciplinary practices in inclusive education: Leadership role of departmental heads in South African schools The South African education system has increasingly progressed in educational access and promoting equity within historically marginalised schooling environments. Despite these reforms, managing learner discipline has become a challenge because it is an under-theorised feature of inclusive education. This study explores the experiences of ten departmental heads (DHs) in implementing inclusive disciplinary practices for learners in digitally evolving classrooms. Underpinned by the inclusive pedagogical theory and transformational leadership theory, this study utilised a qualitative approach within an interpretivist paradigm and a phenomenological design. Data were collected through open-ended questionnaires and semi-structured interviews and analysed through thematic analysis. The findings indicate that although DHs possess robust conceptual understanding of inclusive and restorative discipline, their capacity to implement these practices is limited by systemic and contextual challenges, including entrenched teacher beliefs, resource disparities, policy-practice disjunctions, and escalating administrative demands. title: Exploring how school management teams interpret and implement inclusive education frameworks in resource-constrained settings
text_snippet: Exploring how school management teams interpret and implement inclusive education frameworks in resource-constrained settings South Africa’s inclusive education reforms, articulated through Education White Paper 6 and the SIAS Policy, aim to transform special schools into equitable learning environments. However, persistent gaps between policy ideals and school-level realities raise critical questions about implementation. This study explores how School Management Teams (SMTs) interpret and implement inclusive education frameworks in resource-constrained settings. A qualitative case study design within an interpretivist paradigm was adopted. Data were collected using semi-structured interviews. These were conducted with SMT members, an occupational therapist, and a district official in KwaZulu-Natal. Data analysis employed a thematic approach, guided by adaptive and distributed leadership theories. The findings revealed five key themes: limited knowledge of policy mandates, entrenched systemic barriers, adaptive leadership practices, insufficient professional development, and weak accountability mechanisms. title: Beyond deficit thinking: Towards a holistic and Ubuntu framework for inclusive education
text_snippet: Beyond deficit thinking: Towards a holistic and Ubuntu framework for inclusive education Inclusive education has emerged globally as a transformative response to historical patterns of exclusion and inequality in schooling, aiming to ensure equitable access, participation, and meaningful learning for all learners regardless of disability, socioeconomic status, or cultural background. However, many school practices remain shaped by deficit thinking, particularly the medical model, which locates educational difficulties within individual learners. This conceptual explanatory paper identifies and discusses themes on how inclusive education can move beyond deficit-oriented approaches towards more holistic and Ubuntu-informed frameworks. Adopting a typological design systematically compares three approaches to inclusive education: the medical deficit model, a holistic approach, and an Ubuntu framework, through a critical analysis of relevant literature. The study develops a holistic Ubuntu-informed conceptual framework that clarifies teachers’ roles and responsibilities in diverse inclusive classrooms and focuses on values such as interconnectedness, dignity, and mutual care. title: Reframing digital access, device regulation, and learner participation: A critical review grounded in a social justice framework
text_snippet: Reframing digital access, device regulation, and learner participation: A critical review grounded in a social justice framework The rapid expansion of digital technologies in education has intensified longstanding socioeconomic inequalities globally. In schools, unequal access to digital technologies has introduced new challenges for inclusive participation. This study reports on a qualitative study conducted to critically interrogate this phenomenon. It began with a critical review of existing research on digital access, device regulation, and learner participation. Informed by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) principles, a systematic literature review was conducted. Thirty-two relevant peer-reviewed studies (published between 2020 and 2026) were analysed using a qualitative thematic synthesis approach. Nancy Fraser’s three-dimensional social justice framework, centered on parity of participation, guided the interpretation. From this analysis, a parity-of-digital-participation framework was developed. title: Teacher-student relationships and learner discipline in digital inclusive education: A relational pedagogy perspective from South Africa
text_snippet: Teacher-student relationships and learner discipline in digital inclusive education: A relational pedagogy perspective from South Africa The paradigm shifts from traditional to digital learning has instigated novel challenges for learner discipline, particularly in inclusive classrooms characterised by high levels of student diversity. While the current discourse largely focuses on technological solutions or behavioural management, it has overlooked the role of teacher-student relationships in shaping teacher-student engagement and learner behaviour online. This study argues that relational pedagogy intentionally cultivates caring teacher-student relationships, thus fostering positive student discipline in digitally mediated inclusive educational environments. Drawing on the Attachment Theory (Riley, 2010), the Community of Inquiry Theory (Garrison et al., 2000), and Noddings' (2013) Ethic of Care Theory, the study adopts a qualitative multiple-case study design to determine the perspectives of ten participants (four lecturers and six students) specifically from higher education digital inclusive classrooms in South Africa, demonstrating that the dynamics of learner discipline differ across educational sectors. title: ‘Always Online’: Investigating how the continuous digital connectivity influences academic discipline among postgraduate students at a South African university

Four postgraduate honours students were selected using convenience sampling from the Curriculum Studies Department at a South African university. title: From innovation to inclusion: Advancing equity through AI policy and governance in South African higher education
text_snippet: From innovation to inclusion: Advancing equity through AI policy and governance in South African higher education As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in higher education, empirical evidence on how institutional governance shapes its equitable and responsible implementation in South African universities remains limited. This study examined how institutional policies and governance practices influence the implementation and equitable use of AI in undergraduate education while contributing to international discourse on responsible AI governance. Participants comprised university leaders, academic staff, professional support staff, and undergraduate students involved in or affected by AI governance and implementation. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and document analysis and analysed using thematic analysis supported by inductive coding. title: Policy versus practice: Exploring the state of inclusive education in marginalised urban public schools through a cultural-historical lens
text_snippet: Policy versus practice: Exploring the state of inclusive education in marginalised urban public schools through a cultural-historical lens Although inclusive education was promulgated over two decades ago, research highlights persistent challenges in its implementation, particularly within the mainstream public schooling system serving historically disadvantaged communities. Guided by Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) and anchored on a qualitative research approach, the study explored the state of inclusive education in under-resourced public schools situated in urban marginalised communities. Twelve members of School-Based Support Teams (SBSTs) from two mainstream schools in Soweto were purposively selected. Face-to-face interviews and review of SBST administrative files were used to collect data. Thematic results revealed a fundamental knowledge gap among SBST members, highlighting discrepancies between policy ideals and practice. Results indicated a systemic disjuncture between SBST procedures and District-level support, leaving teachers without adequate support. title: Barriers faced by visually impaired students in using the modular object-oriented dynamic learning environment at a university in Namibia
text_snippet: Barriers faced by visually impaired students in using the modular object-oriented dynamic learning environment at a university in Namibia While Learning Management Systems like Moodle are designed to foster inclusive higher education, visually impaired students at universities in Namibia continue to face severe accessibility barriers due to unoptimised platform design and incompatible course materials. This study investigated the barriers faced by students with visual impairments in utilising the Modular Object-Oriented Dynamic Learning Environment (Moodle) at a university selected in Namibia. It is a qualitative approach that draws on a phenomenological research design. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and non-participant observations with six visually impaired undergraduate students, four lecturers, and three e-learning administrative staff. The data were analysed through thematic analysis. The findings showed that Moodle’s affordances, such as flexible pacing and reduced classroom anxiety, are accompanied by critical accessibility barriers, including poor screen reader compatibility, limited assistive technology, and insufficient institutional support. title: Transforming curriculum for inclusive education: Insights from a university-led professional development programme in South Africa
text_snippet: Transforming curriculum for inclusive education: Insights from a university-led professional development programme in South Africa Despite South Africa's progressive inclusive education policies, such as Education White Paper 6 and the SIAS policy, a significant gap persists between policy ideals and classroom practice, a gap frequently attributed to the inadequate preparation of in-service teachers. While higher education institutions (HEIs) have increasingly offered Continuous Professional Development (CPD) programmes to address this, the curriculum design and effectiveness of these initiatives remain critically under-examined. This study investigates how the curriculum content and structure of a university-led Short Learning Programme (SLP) on inclusive education equips (or fails to equip) in-service teachers with the knowledge, skills, and values required for inclusive practice in South African schools. This qualitative case study was guided by an interpretivist paradigm, seeking to understand participants' lived experiences and meaning-making within their specific contexts. The study employed a case study design to explore the bounded system of the SLP offered by a South African university to in-service teachers. title: Reimagining accounting education in rural South African schools: Collaborative pedagogy for inclusive learning and analytical skill development.
text_snippet: Reimagining accounting education in rural South African schools: Collaborative pedagogy for inclusive learning and analytical skill development. The persistent use of teacher-centered methods in under-resourced rural South African schools creates a significant barrier to equitable participation and the development of higher-order analytical skills in accounting education, particularly for learners from diverse linguistic and socioeconomic backgrounds. This qualitative study, grounded in an interpretive paradigm, explored how collaborative learning strategies can foster inclusive learning environments and enhance the development of analytical skills among Grade 10 learners in three rural secondary schools in the uMgungundlovu district, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Using a participatory research design, the study involved 30 learners and three teachers in collaborative pedagogical interventions. Data were collected through classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, and focus group discussions, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings revealed that structured collaboration not only improved learners’ analytical reasoning and problem-solving skills but also created a more inclusive classroom by redistributing participation, enabling peer scaffolding, and reducing language barriers. text_snippet: Exploring teachers’ lived experiences in addressing learners’ misconduct in secondary schools at the King Cetshwayo district, KwaZulu-Natal Effective classroom management remains a critical element in the South African education system, especially in schools where learners disrupt teaching and learning. This study explored teachers’ lived experiences in addressing learners’ misconduct and the strategies fostering these challenges at secondary schools in the King Cetshwayo district, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. It was guided by Ecological Systems Theory and Social Learning Theory, and used a qualitative phenomenological research design. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews with six teachers purposively selected from secondary schools. These teachers had direct experience managing learners’ behaviour in their classrooms. This study used a complementary document analysis of school disciplinary policies and codes of conduct to strengthen contextual understanding. Data were analysed using thematic analysis, enabling the identification of recurring patterns in teachers’ experiences and classroom management practices. title: Rethinking learner discipline in digital and inclusive education: Bridging theory, policy, and classroom practices.
text_snippet: Rethinking learner discipline in digital and inclusive education: Bridging theory, policy, and classroom practices. Learner discipline has become one of the most contested and evolving areas of educational research and practice. Once largely understood through behaviourist and punitive paradigms, contemporary scholarship increasingly conceptualises learner discipline as a multidimensional process situated at the intersection of educational leadership, inclusive education, learner wellbeing, democratic participation, and organisational development. This conceptual shift reflects profound changes in education systems worldwide, driven by technological innovation, increasing learner diversity, rights-based educational reforms, and growing recognition of the importance of equitable and inclusive learning environments. Consequently, learner discipline can no longer be viewed simply as a mechanism for maintaining order; rather, it constitutes a critical dimension of educational quality that shapes teaching effectiveness, learner engagement, school climate, and institutional improvement.

title: Teacher leadership for effective learner discipline in digital learning and inclusive education: From policy to classroom practice
text_snippet: Teacher leadership for effective learner discipline in digital learning and inclusive education: From policy to classroom practice Although national education policies promote equity, inclusion, learner discipline, and digital integration, limited attention has been given to how teacher preparation equips Foundation Phase teachers to exercise leadership in managing learner discipline in digitally mediated and inclusive classrooms. The study explored how teacher leadership supports effective learner discipline in digital learning and inclusive education contexts by examining teachers’ preparedness and the translation of policy expectations into classroom practice. The study was grounded in an interpretivist paradigm and adopted a qualitative research approach. A multiple-case study design was employed to gain an in-depth understanding of teachers' lived experiences across different school contexts. Six Foundation Phase teachers from three primary schools were purposively selected as participants. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews, which enabled participants to share their views on their preparedness, experiences, and challenges in managing learner discipline in digital and inclusive learning environments. title: Effectiveness of Sesotho folktales on children’s language skills development at a pre-school in the Maseru district, Lesotho: Parents’ and teachers’ perceptions.
text_snippet: Effectiveness of Sesotho folktales on children’s language skills development at a pre-school in the Maseru district, Lesotho: Parents’ and teachers’ perceptions. Folktale is an indigenous pedagogical tool that offers invaluable moral lessons and enhances children's cognitive and language skills. Some countries are considering incorporating cultural activities into the school curriculum to preserve culture and benefit from learning through local cultural resources. This study explored parents' and pre-school teachers' perceptions of the effectiveness of Sesotho folktales in developing children’s language skills in Lesotho. It used a qualitative approach, employing a case study design. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with parents and pre-school teachers at a pre-school in the Maseru district, Lesotho. The data were analysed through thematic analysis. The findings indicate that both parents and teachers highlighted that folktales could positively influence the children’s language skills development. The findings revealed further that the art of folktale narration is disappearing among the Basotho community, as parents and teachers indicated that they do not narrate folktales to their children and learners, respectively. title: Literacy at the crossroad: Early-grade literacy teaching challenges in Zambia’s Chama district
text_snippet: Literacy at the crossroad: Early-grade literacy teaching challenges in Zambia’s Chama district To retain teachers in the profession and encourage them to stay in rural areas, it is essential to recognise the challenges they face. Assisting them in discovering solutions will enhance their classroom practices. This study examines the challenges teachers face in supporting early-grade learners during the mentoring process. The study employed a qualitative case study design. Fifteen participants were purposefully selected from two schools in the Chama district in Zambia. These included one district official, two school head teachers, two senior teachers or mentors, two School in-service coordinators, four early-grade teachers, and four parents. Data for the study were collected through semi-structured focus groups and supplemented by observation. The data gathered were analysed using a thematic analysis approach. The findings revealed several challenges affecting the teaching of early-grade literacy and teacher support and mentoring. Accordingly, the study recommends that appropriate measures be implemented to ensure adequate teacher support and mentoring.

title: Reimagining entrepreneurial education in South African universities to enhance graduate employability
text_snippet: Reimagining entrepreneurial education in South African universities to enhance graduate employability This study examines how entrepreneurial education in South African universities can be redesigned to improve graduate employability. Specifically, the study aims to evaluate how experiential learning, structured mentorship, and university–industry collaboration can better align entrepreneurial education with South Africa’s socio-economic context and developmental needs. This study adopts a qualitative desktop research methodology. Data were collected through a structured review of peer-reviewed journal articles, policy documents, and institutional reports sourced from academic databases, including Google Scholar and accredited open-access journals. The primary data collection instrument was a systematic document review protocol, and the data were analysed using qualitative thematic analysis. The findings revealed four central themes such as weak conversion of entrepreneurial intention into action, limited institutional support for entrepreneurial capacity, outdated pedagogies that inhibit innovation, and a lack of focus on sustainability. title: Exploring the importance of learning support for learners with barriers to learning in senior-phase schools within the King Cetshwayo district
text_snippet: Exploring the importance of learning support for learners with barriers to learning in senior-phase schools within the King Cetshwayo district Barriers to learning in South Africa constitute a critical factor impeding teaching processes and constraining pupils' academic achievement across all educational levels. Regrettably, unresolved debates persist amongst stakeholders regarding how, when, and why to provide necessary learning support to pupils with diverse learning needs. This study explores the significance of learning support for pupils with learning barriers in senior-phase schools within the King Cetshwayo District, examining the availability and challenges of learning support for secondary school pupils who struggle academically, alongside the potential roles of educational stakeholders in providing such support. The study is underpinned by Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, which portrays learning as a social process originating in society and culture, and Bronfenbrenner's bioecological systems theory, which emphasises that multiple environmental systems influence child development. journal_name: International Journal of Studies in Inclusive Education
title: Contextualising and inclusive accounting education through community engagement: Participatory action research in rural South African schools
text_snippet: Contextualising and inclusive accounting education through community engagement: Participatory action research in rural South African schools Accounting education in rural South Africa is marked by a disconnect from local realities and a lack of inclusive pedagogy, leading to disengagement and inequitable outcomes. This study employed a Participatory Action Research (PAR) framework, informed by Situated Learning Theory and Critical Pedagogy, to collaboratively design and test contextually relevant and inclusive accounting activities with educators, learners, and community stakeholders. Co-designed interventions included a differentiated curriculum using local case studies, peer-learning networks for educators, community-based learning projects, and mobile technology to enhance access. The PAR process successfully addressed key challenges of resources and isolation. Results showed significant improvements in learner engagement, academic performance, and the social inclusion of marginalised learners, while also empowering educators. The research demonstrates that contextualisation and inclusion are synergistic goals best achieved through democratic, community-engaged praxis. It provides a validated model for developing resilient and equitable accounting education in diverse, resource-constrained settings.

journal_name: International Journal of Studies in Inclusive Education
title: Teaching learners with learning disabilities in inclusive classrooms in Lesotho: Challenges and opportunities
text_snippet: Teaching learners with learning disabilities in inclusive classrooms in Lesotho: Challenges and opportunities Drawing on lived experiences in Lesotho's primary schools, this paper discusses the challenges educators face in teaching learners with learning disabilities in inclusive classrooms. This study was undertaken using two Mafeteng district schools, namely Primary School and Primary School B. The study found that challenges in teaching learners with LD stem from deficiencies in policies and approaches at the national, school, and classroom levels. This study is a timely intervention intended to add knowledge on how learners with LD can be best supported without compromising the quality of education, demoralising either the teacher or the learner, and, more importantly, attaining what the education system is set to achieve. The most important finding was that teachers face complex challenges in managing inclusive classrooms; therefore, the Ministry of Education and Training should take appropriate action to remedy the prevailing school situation.

title: Exploring senior education specialists’ roles in developing educators at secondary schools in the Gert Sibande education district
text_snippet: Exploring senior education specialists’ roles in developing educators at secondary schools in the Gert Sibande education district Since 1994, the South African education system has been on a transformational trajectory. New curricula, policies, management, and control systems emerged. They heralded a fundamental change in the education system. The education system thus adopted a different outlook, with transformative aims and objectives. In line with this change, the previous school inspectors were renamed Senior Education Specialists (SESs). They were assigned a development role, unlike their predecessors, who were known for coercion, subjugation, dismissiveness, and a tendency to use judgmental approaches in support of schools. This study explores the roles of SESs in developing educators, identifies factors that impede their effectiveness in this development, and suggests strategies they could use to achieve educator development and attain educational goals. It employed a qualitative Case study research design, through which a sample of SESs was interviewed and observed. It employed documents that SESs use in the performance of its developmental support service to educators. title: Exploring the capacity of school-based support teams to promote inclusive education in township schools
text_snippet: Exploring the capacity of school-based support teams to promote inclusive education in township schools This study explored the capacity of School-Based Support Teams (SBSTs) to implement inclusive education through Education White Paper 6 (EWP6) in two township schools in Soweto, Johannesburg. Cultural-Historical Activity Theory guides it. It employed a qualitative approach, utilising a case study research design. Twelve SBST members, comprising three males and nine females, aged between 30 and 63 years, were purposefully selected from primary and secondary schools in Johannesburg North, South Africa. Semi-structured interviews and document analysis of SBST files were employed to generate data. Thematic analysis was used to analyse, which was supported by ATLAS.ti. The findings revealed that SBSTs demonstrated limited conceptual understanding of inclusive education, often reflecting deficit-based perspectives rooted in historical segregationist frameworks. They showed that committees were poorly constituted, operationally weak, and delegated most work to committee chairpersons, with members reporting professional inadequacy and inconsistent training. title: Provision of support structures for beginner teachers at schools: An induction programme approach
text_snippet: Provision of support structures for beginner teachers at schools: An induction programme approach This study explored providing support structures for beginner teachers at schools during the induction programme in the Thabo Mofutsanyane district schools. Entering the teaching profession is a challenge for many beginner teachers. Studies in the South African and international contexts have shown that beginner teachers often experience a lack of support from their colleagues or inadequate mentorship when they enter the teaching profession, which can lead to frustration and even resignation. One aspect that might help beginner teachers overcome this challenge is through the support structures offered through induction programs. Induction programmes are designed to prepare beginner teachers when they enter the workplace. Many such induction programmes in South Africa and internationally have not guided new teachers' objectives in their new positions. A research gap reveals that novice teachers often lack support when they enter the profession. Using an induction programme, this study explored how support structures can be provided to beginner teachers participating in an induction programme. title: Ecological determinants of bullying-induced suicidality: An exploration of ex(in)clusion of mental health in rural primary schools in Zimbabwe
text_snippet: Ecological determinants of bullying-induced suicidality: An exploration of ex(in)clusion of mental health in rural primary schools in Zimbabwe Bullying, a pervasive issue within educational contexts, has been linked to severe psychological distress and suicidal ideation, especially in rural marginalised populations. Despite the significant implications of this phenomenon, there exists a conspicuous research gap concerning the interplay between environmental factors and the mental health outcomes of rural adolescents in Zimbabwe. This study explored the ecological determinants contributing to bullying-induced suicidality, which focuses on the mental health disparities prevalent in rural Zimbabwean primary schools. It employed a qualitative approach and used an exploratory research design. Sixteen participants were purposively selected based on gender, expertise, and age, ensuring a diverse representation of perspectives at rural primary schools in Mazowe district, Zimbabwe. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed through thematic analysis. The findings revealed that the pervasive influence of community norms and peer dynamics exacerbates the mental health challenges faced by learners. title: Teachers’ adaptation of assessment practices for learners with hearing impairments in inclusive schools, Ketu South, Ghana
text_snippet: Teachers’ adaptation of assessment practices for learners with hearing impairments in inclusive schools, Ketu South, Ghana This study examined how teachers adapt assessment practices to meet the learning needs of students with hearing impairments in inclusive basic schools in Ghana. Guided by a qualitative phenomenological design, the research sought to capture teachers’ lived experiences of modifying assessment procedures within inclusive settings. Data were collected through document analysis, classroom observations, and semi-structured interviews with nine teachers purposively selected from six basic schools in the Ketu South Municipality, which are known for enrolling learners who are deaf or hard of hearing. Thematic analysis revealed that teachers implemented various adaptations, including extended assessment time, simplified instructions, and reduced written demands. However, the consistency and quality of these adaptations varied considerably. Some teachers demonstrated limited proficiency in sign language, tailoring question formats, and aligning assessment adjustments with individual learner needs. title: Enhancing critical thinking and problem-solving skills of grade 11 learners in accounting education in high school at uMgungundlovu district, South Africa
text_snippet: Enhancing critical thinking and problem-solving skills of grade 11 learners in accounting education in high school at uMgungundlovu district, South Africa This study presents a framework for enhancing critical thinking and problem-solving skills in grade 11 Accounting. It emphasises the need for high school learners to develop both accounting knowledge and adaptable thinking skills, which are crucial for academic and professional success. In today's dynamic world, critical thinking and problem-solving are invaluable, particularly in accounting, where complex financial challenges are commonplace. High school is a pivotal stage for developing these skills, laying a strong foundation for future careers and professional success. The study employs multifaceted methodology, including literature review, classroom observations, and stakeholder discussions. It identifies effective teaching strategies and curriculum elements that foster critical thinking and problem-solving skills. The proposed educational plan incorporates a range of instructional methods to engage learners. It features real-world case studies, providing practical insights into financial scenarios and requiring creative application of accounting knowledge. title: Leveraging rural teaching strategies from the COVID-19 era to build resilient learning environments: A case study from South Africa
text_snippet: Leveraging rural teaching strategies from the COVID-19 era to build resilient learning environments: A case study from South Africa This study explores how rural teachers and learners in South Africa responded to the educational challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic and how their adaptive strategies can inform long-term, inclusive teaching practices. Grounded in Resilience Theory and Inclusive Pedagogy, the study adopts a qualitative, interpretive phenomenological approach to explore the lived experiences of six learners and two teachers at a quintile one high school in the Maluti-a-Phofung district, Free State province. Data were collected via semi-structured WhatsApp interviews and analysed thematically. Findings highlight four key enablers of resilience: access to basic digital resources, teacher training in technology use, community and parental involvement, and learner adaptability. The study argues that grassroots strategies developed during the crisis offer valuable models for sustainable, equity-focused education in rural contexts beyond the pandemic. These insights contribute to the development of responsive, future-ready schooling systems that prioritise continuity and inclusion.

title: Ubuntu as a lens for navigating complexities in teaching economic and management sciences in rural-based secondary schools
text_snippet: Ubuntu as a lens for navigating complexities in teaching economic and management sciences in rural-based secondary schools Ubuntu is an African philosophical framework emphasising community, interconnectedness, and mutual care. This study identified the unique and specific challenges teachers face in teaching Economic and Management Sciences (EMS). This study investigated the complexities of teaching EMS in rural-based secondary schools through the lens of Ubuntu. Additionally, this study explored how the principles of Ubuntu can be applied to address the identified challenges and enhance EMS teaching and learning in rural secondary schools. Consequently, a purposive sampling procedure was used to select 16 grade 8 and 9 teachers who were part of the Community Engagement project to generate data. Qualitative questionnaire instruments were used to gather data. Moreover, the data were analysed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed that applying the principles of Ubuntu can foster a more supportive and cohesive educational environment, thereby enhancing both teacher effectiveness and learner engagement. journal_name: International Journal of Studies in Inclusive Education
title: Exploring the influence of absent father figures on the sexual behaviours of male orphan learners in rural schools
text_snippet: Exploring the influence of absent father figures on the sexual behaviours of male orphan learners in rural schools This study explores the absence of fathers' influence on sexual abuse among female learners at rural communities in Zaka South district. The absence of fathers in the lives of children could influence the behaviours among male orphan children”. This study employs a qualitative approach, utilising a case study research design. Eighteen participants were purposively selected to ensure balanced representation across gender, expertise, geographical location, and age. Two focus group discussions were conducted for data collection, including one with learners with disabilities and another with adults. Thematic analysis was used to analyse data. The finding indicates that the absence of a paternal presence profoundly affects the emotional and behavioural development of male orphans, often resulting in maladaptive behaviours that can escalate into sexually abusive actions. This study recommends establishing mentorship programmes to connect male orphans with positive male role models, which may reduce maladaptive behaviours and foster healthier interpersonal relationships.
